title: Foundations of Psychological Research
text:
Welcome
Welcome to PSYC4242!
How do we decide whether two groups differ in a psychological process or behaviour? This module builds on the knowledge and skills acquired in Introduction to Psychological Research (PSYC4141). You will continue to build your understanding of rigorous and transparent scientific practices and develop your thinking of real-world issues. Using modern techniques, learn more about how to collect, present and analyse data. You will be introduced to key concepts and practices of research design and data analysis through lectures. Practical laboratory classes will teach you how to design studies, handle data, perform statistical analyses and report your findings. The laboratory classes will be hands-on, giving you direct experience with all stages of a research project, including the use of specialised software. Topics covered will include experimental design, how to decide on your study participants, comparing groups for behaviours of psychological interest and hypothesis testing.


Asking for help
We have carefully prepared and refined the lab materials in this course over several years, and we feel that the pace of the materials is just right for our students. Some students will complete them more quickly, and others more slowly - both of these scenarios are absolutely fine. You should work at the pace that suits you best, making sure you understand the materials before you move forward.
It is fairly inevitable that you will get stuck on the lab materials in this module at some point. This might be in Week 11, Week 12, or later. When you do, it’s important you reach out for help:

Ask your peers on your table. We’ve designed this teaching space to help collaborative work. You are encouraged to work with other students. Make sure you ask others to explain how they’ve solved an exercise. Make sure you help out others where you can. Always make sure you understand the code and the exercise; don’t simply be satisfied that you’ve got the right answer.
Ask a Lecturer. We are here to help you. There are no “stupid questions” in statistics, so just ask the Lecturer any question about what you’re doing.
Ask on the Q&A Forum on Moodle. On the PSYC4242 moodle page you will find a Q&A Forum. This is a great way to ask a question outside of the lab sessions. It might seem scary to ask a question in the forum, but please don’t be afraid to do this. If you have a question, you can bet 30+ other students also have the same question! So by asking the question on the forum, you help out many more people on the module. A friendly GTA or Lecturer will be along to answer the question as soon as possible (we aim for within 48 hours during the working week).
Ask during live online Q & A session. Each week we hold an online “Q&A” session where we will try and resolve any general queries and problems. It’s an ideal time to discuss things that students are struggling with or confused about. You can ask on the discussion forum above and then we might be able to pick up the issues and discuss them, but you can also ask in the session itself.

title: How to build a plot
text:
Overview

What is a Quarto document and how do we use it?
How to run code to read in data and build a plot


In this video we’ll talk about what a Quarto document is and we’ll start looking at how you can use it. I’ll also walk through how we use code to get R to read in data and build a plot

title: How to build a plot
text:
Step 2: Setup - load libraries

library(here)
library(tidyverse)


The here package helps with finding your files.
The tidyverse is a set of packages that handles almost everything you need to do with data.

Learn more about the tidyverse here: https://tidyverse.org

title: How to build a plot
text:
Step 3: Reading in the data

data_mw <- read_csv(here("PSYC4141/files/week1/", "data_bmw3.csv"))


read_csv is function that reads in data that are stored in a file of the type .csv. We need to tell R where the file is and what it is called.

<- is an assignment arrow, telling R that we want to put the data in an object (or dataframe) called data_mw

title: How to build a plot
text:
Step 4: Build the plot

CodePlot



ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01))


We use ggplot() to tell R that we want to create a plot and we tell R the data the use and the variable to plot

title: How to build a plot
text:
Step 4: a simple histogram

CodePlot



ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01)) +   
  geom_histogram()


We tell R what type of plot to use


If you just had the code on line 1, you would not see a plot. You have to tell R what type of plot to use. Here we’ll use a ‘histogram’, so we tell it to use the geometric object ‘histogram’. There are many different types of geometric objects. We’ll encounter a few during this module. Plus adds a layer

title: How to build a plot
section: Step 4: Build the plot - different background
text:
Step 4: Build the plot - different background

CodePlot



ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01)) +
  geom_histogram()  +                                     
  theme_bw()                                             


Changes the background


There are many different themes. Here I’ve gone for a simple black and white theme. Note: layer

title: How to build a plot
section: Step 4: Build the plot - change the colours of the bars
text:
Step 4: Build the plot - change the colours of the bars

CodePlot



ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01, fill = "tomato")) + 
  geom_histogram()  + 
  theme_bw()


Specify an additional bit of code (or argumment) inside the mapping part of the function ggplot(). Instead of using the default grey, I’m telling R to ‘fill in’ the bars with a tomato red.

title: How to build a plot
section: Step 4: Build the plot - remove the legend
text:
Step 4: Build the plot - remove the legend

CodePlot



ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01, fill = "tomato")) + 
  geom_histogram()  + 
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")


Removes the legend

title: How to build a plot
section: Step 4: Build the plot - change the title of the x-axis
text:
Step 4: Build the plot - change the title of the x-axis

CodePlot



ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01, fill = "tomato")) + 
  geom_histogram()  + 
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "Brief Mind Wandering Three-Factor Scale - Question 1")


Adds a more informative title for the x-axis.

title: How to build a plot
section: Step 4: Build the plot - change the value labels
text:
Step 4: Build the plot - change the value labels

CodePlot



ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01, fill = "tomato")) + 
  geom_histogram()  + 
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  labs(x = "Brief Mind Wandering Three-Factor Scale - Question 1") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 0:4,
    labels = c("Fully disagree", "Somewhat disagree", "Neutral", "Somewhat agree", "Fully agree")
  )

Lines 6. to 9. Replaces numerical values with text labels

title: 2. Week 2 - Measuring, describing, and visualising psychological concepts
text:
Overview



This week we focus on two strands of learning:
A. Psychological measurement - how we turn psychological concepts into measurable data, and how we can summarise those data using numbers. B. Variability and distributions - why differences between people and observations matter, and how we can measure and visualise information that a single average might hide.
The materials we have prepared to support your learning are arranged in four parts:

Lectures
Reading
Pre-lab activities
Lab activities

You can navigate to each in the side bar on the right

title: 2. Week 2 - Measuring, describing, and visualising psychological concepts
text:
Lectures
Last week, you looked at some of the bigger questions that sit behind psychological science: how theories are linked to observable evidence, why our observations provide estimates rather than direct access to the “truth”, and why the complexity and variability of human behaviour matter.
This week, we move from those ideas to some of the practical tools that allow us to gather and make sense of evidence. We’ll look at how psychological concepts can be represented as data, and how choices about measurement, summary and visualisation shape the evidence we use to evaluate scientific claims.
The lectures are grouped into section A and B (relating to the two strands of learning stated above). Each section is split into short videos so you can work through them at your own pace. It’s a good idea to take notes as you go and to have a 10-minute break between section A and section B.
:::{.callout-note title=“A note about the recordings”} The recordings were originally delivered by Prof John Towse and have been selected and reorganised for this week’s teaching. If you hear references to a different week or to something covered “last week” don’t worry about these references! I’ve reviewed the materials and you will never be expected to know anything that you haven’t yet covered. All questions should be posted on the discussion forum and will be answered by Carly. Please do not contact John about his content. :::






Questions?



Make a note of questions as you work through the material. These might be answered later in the recordings, or in your lab. Otherwise, please bring them to the live online Q&A session on Friday or post them on the Q&A forum on Moodle.



Section A: Psychological measurement and central tendency
You can watch the lecture for the video using the video playback windows shown next. Section A is broken into three parts that should be watched in sequence:

Types of data
Scales of measurement
Central tendency and notations

Download the slides for sections A and B in one go here. The transcript for all the videos is here.
1. Types of data (~10 minutes)
What types of data can we use to measure psychological concepts that we are interested in? This includes nominal and numerical data.

2. Scales of Measurement (~9 minutes) Four different scales that we commonly use to measure our data. These include nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio.

3. Measures of central tendency and key notations (~10 minutes) Why measurement matters, and how to describe your data using numbers and appropriate measures. This includes the mean, median and mode.

:::{callout-tip title=“Take a break!”} Before continuing, we recommend you take a 15-minute break away from your computer. Remember to note down any questions to bring to the Q&A, lab or discussion forum whilst you’re watching the lectures. :::


Section B: Variability and distributions
Section B is broken into four parts that should be watched in sequence:

Variability in numbers
Variability in words
The standard deviation and distribution curves
The normal distribution curve

1. Variability in numbers (~19 minutes) Why does variability or ‘spread’ in our data matter? How can we measure and express variability using numbers? This includes range, interquartile range, deviance, variance and standard deviation.

2. Variability in words (~5 minutes) A short reflection on what numerical measures of variability can actually tell us about our data.

:::{callout-tip title=“Formulae and calculations”} John has just introduced the notion of using calculations to measure variability and the broader concepts behind them. You can download the key formulae for calculating variance and standard deviation and other measures here You may come across slightly different versions of these formulae (computational and conceptual) so it is useful to be aware of them. You do not need to memorise these formulae. The important thing is to understand what each measure tells us about our data and the basic idea behind how it is calculated. In the next recording, John will take you through a worked example of calculating a standard deviation. :::
3. The standard deviation and distribution curves (~15 minutes) An example of how to calculate standard deviation, and how we can look at variability visually using histogram plots. An overview of the shape of data distributions, with features including symmetry, skew, and bimodality.

4. The normal distribution (~9 minutes) Basic properties of the normal distribution curve and linking central tendency and standard deviation to the normal curve.

Reading






Easy access to readings



All reading is accessible via the library. You can go to Moodle -> Library Resources -> Resource List or you can follow this link. Readings have one of the following tags:

Essential: We expect you to be familiar with these reading. You will be assessed on this.
Recommended: We highly recommend these readings. They often provide a different perspective, or explain things in a different way.
Optional: Further readings for those interested.

The reading list is divided into multiple sections:

Reading associated with statistics: this contains links to readings useful for the development of statistical concepts and skills. The main textbook Fundamental statistics for the behavioral sciences by Howell (Essential) lives here.
Reading associated with psychological research principles and design: this contains links to readings that provide a good basis for foundational knowledge around research design.
Reading associated with Open Science principles and practices: this contains links to key literature on the Open Science movement.
Week by week: these contain links to key reading for that week that are not listed on any of the more general lists above.



For week 2, the reading is:

Keck, S., & Tang, W. (2020). Enhancing the wisdom of the crowd with cognitive-process diversity: The benefits of aggregating intuitive and analytical judgments. Psychological Science, 31(10), 1272-1282. Essential
Lorenz, J., Rauhut, H., Schweitzer, F., & Helbing, D. (2011). How social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America, 108(22), 9020–9025. Recommended
Howell, D. C. (2017). Fundamental statistics for the behavioral sciences (9th ed.). Cengage Learning. Chapters 2, 4, 5 and 6. Recommended

title: 2. Week 2 - Measuring, describing, and visualising psychological concepts
text:
Pre-lab activities
The lecture mateerial is designed to deliver important ideas and procedures for learning about psychological science and analysis. Pre-lab material is then designed to help consolidate this learning, or enhance, expand and apply it in ways that set the scene for the lab session activity. We want to prepare you to be ready to go in the session itself and make the most of your time there.
Information about a pre-lab activity will be added soon.

Pre-lab activity 1: From psychological claims to measurements
Last week, you considered psychological claims that we might encounter in everyday life. One example is the claim that “screen time negatively impacts mental health in adolescents”. Before we could investigate this claim, we would need to decide what we actually mean by screen time and how we could turn that concept into something we can observe and measure.
One simple approach might be to ask people: “Approximately how many hours did you spend looking at a screen yesterday?”
Imagine we asked a small group of adolescents and received the following sample of responses:
6 8 5 9 7 4 11 6 7 8 10 5 6 12 7 8 4 9 6 7 14 5 8 6 10 7 3 9
Take a moment to think about what these numbers actually represent.






Pre-lab question 1




What scale of measurement best describes the number of hours of screen time reported here?


Nominal
Ordinal
Interval
Ratio







Show answer





d. Ratio. Time measured in hours has equal intervals, and zero hours represents the absence of the measured quantity. This means that differences and ratios between values are meaningful.





Once we have collected observations like these, how can we describe them in a useful way? One way is to summarise the data to find the mean or average value. You’ll learn how to do that in RStudio during the lab, but for now, have a look at this website: https://istats.shinyapps.io/EDA_quantitative/. The website ‘Describing and Exploring Quantitative Variables’ should open in a new window. You may be offered a free trial of the ‘Art of Stat Mobile App’; you can dismiss that.
Choose the following options:

Under ‘Enter Data’, select ‘Your Own’
Under ‘Name of Variable’, enter a sensible label (such as ‘Screen time’)
Under ‘Enter observations’, add the numbers of the observations
Under ‘Choose Type of Plot’, click the box to select a ‘Histogram’.

Now have a look:

On the right, you’ll see key descriptive statistics such as the mean and the standard deviation (Std. Dev.).
Below it, you can see a histogram.







What is a histogram?



A histogram is a graph that shows how the values of a continuous (or finely measured) variable are distributed. The values are divided into consecutive, equal-width intervals called bins, and a bar is drawn for each bin with its height showing how many observations fall inside it (or the proportion or density). Because the bins are adjacent, the bars touch, which distinguishes a histogram from a bar chart of separate categories. Histograms make it easy to see the shape of a distribution, including its centre, spread, skew, and any outliers or multiple peaks.


Play around:

What happens if you add more observations? How does it change the mean and the standard deviation? What happens to the histogram?
Try adding 10 observations of lower screen time values.
Try adding an impossible large observation (like 89).
You can also click the option to see a boxplot as well as a histogram. Can you work out how key descriptive statistics are represented in a boxplot?







Pre-lab question 2




The mean reported screen time in this sample was approximately 7.4 hours. Which of the following would NOT be justified from these data?


Participants reported an average of 7.4 hours of screen time.
There was variation in reported screen time between participants.
Adolescents who use screens more have poorer mental health.
Some participants reported more screen time than others.







Show answer





c. Here, our measure of screen time is self-reported hours of screen use on one day. We have not measured mental health, so these observations cannot tell us whether greater screen use is associated with poorer mental health. Our measure of “screen time” is also only one possible way of representing a complex behaviour. For example, it does not distinguish between different activities or content, such as studying, gaming, messaging friends or watching videos. This illustrates an important challenge in psychological science: the questions and theories we are interested in are often complex, while the data we collect are particular observations produced by the choices we make about what and how to measure. So, even when we can accurately describe a set of observations, we still need to be careful about what those observations allow us to conclude.











Pre-lab question 3




If two sets of data have exactly the same mean, what can we conclude about their variability?



They must have the same variability
They must have the same standard deviation
One must have a larger range
We cannot tell from the mean alone







Show answer





d.







Pre-lab activity 2: Revisit the video on how to get started in RStudio
RStudio is the software that we’ll use to work with data, visualise data and analyse data. It is an important tool when learning to do psychological science.
If you haven’t watched it yet, or would like to remind yourself, please revisit last week’s video on ?@sec-4141-w1-lectures-intro-how-r: How to get started with RStudio.

title: Introduction to Psychological Research
text:
Welcome
Welcome to the PSYC4141 material for the academic year 2026-2027!
How do we determine what is a true finding in psychological science? How do we know which theories are well supported by evidence? This module introduces you to rigorous and transparent scientific practices. You will develop systematic ways of thinking about and approaching real-world issues. Using modern techniques, you will learn how to collect, present and analyse data. We will introduce key concepts and practices of research design and data analysis through lectures. Practical laboratory classes will teach you how to design studies, handle data, perform statistical analyses and report your findings. The laboratory classes will be hands-on, giving you direct experience of all stages of a research project, including the use of specialised software. Topics covered will include questionnaire design, collecting and working with observational data, and looking at relationships between variables using correlation and regression analysis.


Working at your own pace and seeking help
We have carefully prepared and refined the lab materials in this course over several years, and we feel that the pace of the materials is just about right for our students. Some students will complete them more quickly, and others more slowly - both of these scenarios are absolutely fine. You should work at the pace that suits you best, making sure you understand the materials before you move forward.
It is fairly inevitable that you will get stuck on the lab materials in this module at some point. This might be in Week 1, Week 2, or later. When you do, it’s important you reach out for help:

Ask your friends on your table. We’ve designed this teaching space to help collaborative work. You are encouraged to work with other students. Make sure you ask others to explain how they’ve solved an exercise. Make sure you help out others where you can. Always make sure you understand the code and the exercise; don’t simply be satisfied that you’ve got the right answer.
Ask a GTA or Lecturer. Our Graduate Teaching Assistants are there to help you. There are no “stupid questions” in statistics, so just ask the GTAs any question about what you’re doing. Likewise, ask the Lecturer.
Ask on the Q&A Forum on Moodle. On the PSYC4141 moodle page you will find a Q&A Forum. This is a great way to ask a question outside of the lab sessions. It might seem scary to ask a question in the forum, but please don’t be afraid to do this. If you have a question, you can bet 30+ other students also have the same question! So by asking the question on the forum, you help out many more people on the module. A friendly GTA or Lecturer will be along to answer the question as soon as possible (we aim for within 48 hours during the working week).
Ask during live online Q & A session. Each week we hold an online “Q&A” session where we will try and resolve any general queries and problems. It’s an ideal time to discuss things that students are struggling with or confused about, and can share ideas and answers. You can ask on the discussion forum above and then we might be able to pick up the issues and discuss them, but also you can ask in the session itself.

Asking good questions - It’s really important that you give us as much information as you can when you ask your questions (in class and especially on the forum). It’s so much harder to help respond to “I can’t do Exercise 5 in Week 7” (because we don’t know why it is that you can’t do it) than for example “In Exercise 5 of Week 7, I’ve managed to read in the data, but the graph looks quite odd. Here is the code I’m using…”

title: 4141-w1-lab_act1
text: We’ve all been there: you may be trying to focus on a lecture, but a thought on what you would like to have for lunch pops into your mind. Mind wandering describes the common experience of one’s thoughts driting away form the task at hand towards self-generated thoughts and feelings (Smallwood & Schooler, 2006). Today, we’ll work with some publicly available data from a research project on mind wandering. Anna Schubert and colleagues (Schubert et al., 2024) conducted a study in which they created a 12-item questionnaire that measures how often your mind wanders without meaning to, how often you let it wander on purpose, and how aware you are when it happens.

title: 4141-w1-lab_act1
text:
Aims of the activity
We are going to:

Download the data
Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio
Read in the data
Build a plot and make it look nice







Watch the ‘How to’ video



If you haven’t done so already, this is a good time to watch the ‘How to’ video on the handbook page on ‘How to build a plot’.

title: 4141-w1-lab_act1
text:
Step 1: Download the files
To complete this lab activity you will need two files:

We’ll work with an example script called 4141_wk1_lab_act1.qmd. This is a Quarto document.
We need a data file called data_bmw3.csv. This is a file that contains the responses of the participants in one of the studies reported on in the paper by Schubert et al. (2024). It is a file of the type .csv. This means that individual bits of data are separated by comma’s. We’ll often use .csv files.

You can download the files from the handbook (see Step 1 under Lab activity). Usually they will be saved in your ‘Downloads’ folder.

title: 4141-w1-lab_act1
text:
Step 2: Setup
Before we can do anything, we need tell R what packages we want to use. You may wonder what a package is. If R is your kitchen with basic equipment, a package is a specialist cookbook that adds new recipes. All the packages that you’ll need have already been installed on the R-server, but you have to tell R which cookbooks to get off the shelf for what you want to do right now. We use the function library() to do that. It is useful to have a section at the top of your script where you get all the cookbooks you need for this script off the shelf (…or load all the relevant libraries).
The code (or instructions to R) to load the libraries is in the bit below. This is called a ‘code chunk’. You can run the code in the chunk by clicking on the green arrow in the top right corner of the code chunk.

Action: Run the code below to load the libraries.


library(here) # the 'here' package helps with finding your files

here() starts at /Users/margrietgroen/stats/2627_year1

library(tidyverse) # the 'tidyverse' is a set of packages that handles almost everything you need to do with data

Warning: package 'ggplot2' was built under R version 4.4.3


Warning: package 'tidyr' was built under R version 4.4.3

title: 4141-w1-lab_act1
text:
Step 3: Reading in the data
The next step is to read in a data file. Here we’ll use a subset of the data collected by Schubert and colleagues. It contains responses from 215 students on a questionnaire that measures mind wandering. It is a file of the type .csv, so we’ll use the function read_csv() to do this. Inside the function, we tell R where to find the file. This is the bit that comes after here(): PSYC4141/files/week1/; it specifies the filepath. After the comma, we tell R what the file is called, including the extension (data_bmw3.csv). Both of these bits (where it is and what it is called) need to be in double quotation marks (““).

Action: Run the code below to read in the data


data_mw <- read_csv(here("4141_wk1_lab/", "data_bmw3.csv"))

Rows: 215 Columns: 22
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (4): location, type, gender, education
dbl (18): subject, id, Age, BMW3_UN_01, BMW3_UN_02, BMW3_UN_03, BMW3_UN_04, ...

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


You may wonder what the bit is that comes before read_csv(). There we have the name of the object we are assigning the data file to. I’ve called it data, but you can give it any name you like. The <- in between is called an assignment arrow. It basically means that R puts the content of the data file data_bmw3.csv stored at location PSYC4141/files/week1 in an object called data. Once you’ve run the code, you should see it in your Environment (top right quadrant).

title: 4141-w1-lab_act1
text:
Step 4: Build a plot
Now we are ready to create our first plot. Let’s say we’d like to visualise how many people selected each response option for question 1 of the questionnaire. Question 1 was “While listening to a presentation, my thoughts start to trail off unintentionally.” Participants were asked to decide to what extent they agreed or disagreed with that statement. They chose one of the following options: “Fully disagree”, “Somewhat disagree”, “Neutral”, “Somewhat agree” or “Fully agree”.
We can do that by creating a histogram. The function we use for that (and for a lot of other plots you’ll make for research methods and stats) is ggplot(). Inside the function we tell R which data to use and which variable to map onto the x-axis of the histogram.

Action 4a: Run the code below to create a histogram


ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01)) +   # specifies data and variable to plot
  geom_histogram()                                        # specifies what type of plot

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









In a histogram, the height of the bar indicates the number of observations, in this case the number of people that chose each response option. For example, almost 100 people chose option 3.
Now, this does the job, but it doesn’t quite look the way I’d like it to look. Let’s change that. I don’t particularly like the grey background. I can change that by adding a layer to the plot specifying a different background. There are lots of different ‘themes’ in ggplot() that you can use. Have a look at https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html.

Action 4b: Run the code below see the change in background


ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01)) + # specifies data and variable to plot
  geom_histogram()  +                                     # specifies what type of plot
  theme_bw()                                              # changes the background

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









I would like the bars to be red instead of grey. I can make that happen, by specifying an additional bit of code (or ‘argument’ in the ggplot() part. There are lots of different colours and colour schemes available within ggplot(). Have a look at this overview and choose one you like for your plot. There is more to say about which colour schemes to use, but we’ll save that for another day.

Action 4c: Run the code below to change the colour of the bars


ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01, fill = "tomato")) + # ...and makes the bars red
  geom_histogram()  +                                                      # specifies what type of plot
  theme_bw()                                                               # changes the background

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









To avoid the legend on the right getting printed (because we don’t need it in this case), we can tell R not to include it.

Action 4d: Run the code below to remove the legend


ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01, fill = "tomato")) + # ...and makes the bars red
  geom_histogram()  +                                                      # specifies what type of plot
  theme_bw() +                                                             # changes the background
  theme(legend.position = "none")                                          # removes the legend

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









Now, it would be good to have a more informative label for what we’ve plotted on the x-axis. Instead of the variable name BMW3_UN_01, we’ll add ‘Brief Mind Wandering Three-factor Scale - Question 1’.

Action 4e: Run the code below to change the title of the x-axis


ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01, fill = "tomato")) + # ...and makes the bars red
  geom_histogram()  +                                                      # specifies what type of plot
  theme_bw() +                                                             # changes the background
  theme(legend.position = "none") +                                        # removes the legend
  labs(x = "Brief Mind Wandering Three-Factor Scale - Question 1")        # add more informative title for the x-axis

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









Finally, instead of the numerical values 0 to 4 that are currently on the x-axis, we’ll add the labels that are associated with each of these values.

Action 4f: Run the code below to change the value labels


ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01, fill = "tomato")) + # ...and makes the bars red
  geom_histogram()  +                                                      # specifies what type of plot
  theme_bw() +                                                             # changes the background
  theme(legend.position = "none") +                                        # removes the legend
  labs(x = "Brief Mind Wandering Three-Factor Scale - Question 1") +       # add more informative label for the x-axis
  scale_x_continuous(                                                      # replace numerical values with text labels
    breaks = 0:4,
    labels = c("Fully disagree", "Somewhat disagree", "Neutral", "Somewhat agree", "Fully agree")
  )

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









That’s it! You have created your first plot.
For more practice, go through the same steps for a different question.

text:
Lectures

What this module is about: begin here
Introduction to the module (~18 minutes)
Watch this part first. It gives an overview of what the module is about, how the module is organised, how you’ll be assessed and how you can ask for help. The video has captions, in case you find that helpful. You can download the slides and a transcript from the links below the video.

    


Intro slides
Intro transcript



Interactive lecture – Being a scientist, doing a science: watch this to get started on learning and thinking about what we are going to be doing in Psychology
You can watch the lecture for the video using the video playback windows shown next. The lecture is broken into five parts, each about 15 minutes long (some a bit longer).

Big ideas, difficult questions
The hardest science
The logic, the challenges
Science is a thing that is done by people
Science is a social activity: fads, inequities and biases







Tip



During the lecture, we suggest some questions you can think about. Responding to these questions will help you to learn.
It would be great if you cared to enter your questions to me (Rob) about the lecture. You can do that anonymously by clicking on this link and typing in your thoughts:
https://app.sli.do/event/gChjffSSfLvkAJSr9GNuCA
In our practical classes in Week 1, we will return to three questions as part of our opening discussions:

What psychological claims do you see online are pseudoscientific?
How do you recognize if you are looking at credible science?
What is the next revolution for psychological science? Are we already there?



This is a quick (~4 minutes) walk through of how you can watch the video lecture, with tips on how to make playback accessible and convenient.

    

You can download the lecture slides as a .html file you can open in any browser.
The slides end with a references list but don’t worry about reading what’s in the references list, we give you recommended readings in Section 2.






Tip



The slides presented in the next videos can be downloaded as a web page: doing-being-science.html.

Lecture slides

When you download the file, double click on it to open it in your usual web browser for viewing.


Next, you can see the lecture elements. We recommend that you watch them in sequence.

Big ideas, difficult questions (~17 minutes). What is science, how do we do it?


    


The hardest science (~15 minutes). Why learning about people is hard, and why revolutionary new ways of doing psychological science are our response to the challenges.


    


The logic, the challenges (~25 minutes). The logic of the scientific method, and the challengesin doing science when it involves trying to understand people.


    
 

Science is a thing that is done by people (~18 minutes). How is it that groups of people who may not know or like or trust each other can produce this thing: science?

 
    


Science is a social activity: fads, inequities and biases (15 minutes). What do we study? Who does the studying? Fads, inequities and biases, and taking responsibility.


    



Getting started with your practical work: you need this for the labs

How to work with R-Studio (~15 minutes)


    


RStudio walkthrough transcript

text:
Reading






Easy access to readings



All reading is accessible via the library. You can go to Moodle -> Library Resources -> Resource List or you can follow this link. Readings have one of the following tags:

Essential: We expect you to be familiar with these reading. You will be assessed on this.
Recommended: We highly recommend these readings. They often provide a different perspective, or explain things in a different way.
Optional: Further readings for those interested.

The reading list is divided into multiple sections:

Reading associated with statistics: this contains links to readings useful for the development of statistical concepts and skills. The main textbook Fundamental statistics for the behavioral sciences by Howell (Essential) lives here.
Reading associated with psychological research principles and design: this contains links to readings that provide a good basis for foundational knowledge around research design.
Reading associated with Open Science principles and practices: this contains links to key literature on the Open Science movement.
Week by week: these contain links to key reading for that week that are not listed on any of the more general lists above.



For week 1, the reading is:

McMillan, B. T. M., Baumgartner, H.A., Bergmann, C. et al. (2026). What 5000 babies can tell us about developing minds and how to study them. Communications Psychology, 4, 1-5. Essential
Peterson, D. (2016). The baby factory: Difficult research objects, disciplinary standards, and the production of statistical significance. Socius, 2, 1-10. Recommended
Wright, D. B., Barnett, J., & Breakwell, G. M. (2020). Psychology as a science: What is science? In G. M. Breakwell, D. B. Wright, & J. Barnett (Eds.), Research methods in psychology (5th ed., pp. 119–138). SAGE Publications. Recommended

title: 1. Week 1 - Being a scientist, doing a science
text:
Lab activities

Lab activity 1: Reading in data and creating a plot

Background
We’ve all been there: you may be trying to focus on a lecture, but a thought on what you would like to have for lunch pops into your mind. Mind wandering describes the common experience of one’s thoughts drifting away from the task at hand towards self-generated thoughts and feelings (Smallwood & Schooler, 2006). Today, we’ll work with some publicly available data from a research project on mind wandering. Anna Schubert and colleagues (Schubert et al., 2024) conducted a study in which they created a 12-item questionnaire that measures how often your mind wanders without meaning to, how often you let it wander on purpose, and how aware you are when it happens. You can have a look at the questionnaire here.


Aims of the activity
We are going to:

Download the files
Setup the appropriate bits and pieces in RStudio
Read in the data
Build a plot







Watch the ‘How to’ lecture



If you haven’t done so already, this is a good time to watch the ‘How to’ video (here Section 1.3) on ‘How to build a plot’.




Step 1: Download the files
To complete this lab activity you will need two files:

We’ll work with an example script called 4141_wk1_lab_act1.qmd. This is a Quarto document.
We need a data file called data_bmw3.csv. This is a file that contains the responses of the participants in one of the studies reported on in the paper by Schubert et al. (2024). It is a file of the type .csv. This means that individual bits of data are separated by comma’s. We’ll often use .csv files.

You can download the files here: 4141_wk1_lab.zip. Usually they will be saved in your ‘Downloads’ folder.
Next, upload the zip-folder as it is to your Files space on the R-server (bottom right quadrant; no need to extract the files first).
Finally, open the example script by clicking on the file called 4141_wk1_lab_act1.qmd in the Files space on the R-server.


Steps 2, 3 and 4
For steps 2, 3 and 4, you’ll be working in RStudio.
References

text:
Step 2: Setup
Before we can do anything, we need tell R what packages we want to use. You may wonder what a package is. If R is your kitchen with basic equipment, a package is a specialist cookbook that adds new recipes. All the packages that you’ll need have already been installed on the R-server, but you have to tell R which cookbooks to get off the shelf for what you want to do right now. We use the function library() to do that. It is useful to have a section at the top of your script where you get all the cookbooks you need for this script off the shelf (…or load all the relevant libraries).
The code (or instructions to R) to load the libraries is in the bit below. This is called a ‘code chunk’. You can run the code in the chunk by clicking on the green arrow in the top right corner of the code chunk.

Action: Run the code below to load the libraries.


library(here) # the 'here' package helps with finding your files

title: 4141-w1-lab_act1
text:
Step 3: Reading in the data
The next step is to read in a data file. Here we’ll use a subset of the data collected by Schubert and colleagues. It contains responses from 215 students on a questionnaire that measures mind wandering. It is a file of the type .csv, so we’ll use the function read_csv() to do this. Inside the function, we tell R where to find the file. This is the bit that comes after here(): 4141_wk1_lab; it specifies the filepath. After the comma, we tell R what the file is called, including the extension (data_bmw3.csv). Both of these bits (where it is and what it is called) need to be in double quotation marks (““).

Action: Run the code below to read in the data


data_mw <- read_csv(here("4141_wk1_lab", "data_bmw3.csv"))

Rows: 215 Columns: 22
── Column specification ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Delimiter: ","
chr  (4): location, type, gender, education
dbl (18): subject, id, Age, BMW3_UN_01, BMW3_UN_02, BMW3_UN_03, BMW3_UN_04, ...

ℹ Use `spec()` to retrieve the full column specification for this data.
ℹ Specify the column types or set `show_col_types = FALSE` to quiet this message.


You may wonder what the bit is that comes before read_csv(). There we have the name of the object we are assigning the data file to. I’ve called it data, but you can give it any name you like. The <- in between is called an assignment arrow. It basically means that R puts the content of the data file data_bmw3.csv stored at location 4141_wk1_lab in an object called data_mw. Once you’ve run the code, you should see it in your Environment (top right quadrant).

text:
Step 4: Build a plot
Now we are ready to create our first plot. Let’s say we’d like to visualise how many people selected each response option for question 1 of the questionnaire. Question 1 was “While listening to a presentation, my thoughts start to trail off unintentionally.” Participants were asked to decide to what extent they agreed or disagreed with that statement. They chose one of the following options: “Fully disagree”, “Somewhat disagree”, “Neutral”, “Somewhat agree” or “Fully agree”.
We can do that by creating a histogram. The function we use for that (and for a lot of other plots you’ll make for research methods and stats) is ggplot(). Inside the function we tell R which data to use and which variable to map onto the x-axis of the histogram.

Action 4a: Run the code below to create a histogram


ggplot(data = data_mw, mapping = aes(x = BMW3_UN_01)) +   # specifies data and variable to plot
  geom_histogram()                                        # specifies what type of plot

`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.









In a histogram, the height of the bar indicates the number of observations, in this case the number of people that chose each response option. For example, almost 100 people chose option 3.
Now, this does the job, but it doesn’t quite look the way I’d like it to look. Let’s change that. I don’t particularly like the grey background. I can change that by adding a layer to the plot specifying a different background. There are lots of different ‘themes’ in ggplot() that you can use. Have a look at https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html.
